meta.topic: Incorrect EMI for a small customer subset

problem:
Aldergate Bank has received complaints from a small group of loan customers: their monthly EMI is wrong. Most customers are unaffected, which makes the problem harder, not easier. The complaints share a pattern that only emerges when the cases are compared: the affected loans were taken out on particular dates, some have a rate change in their history, and a few have a part-payment that the schedule did not handle. The lending team suspects a rounding error, the product team suspects the rate table, and the operations team suspects the customer data. Each theory explains some cases and none explains all of them.

The learner must trace the calculation from its inputs to its output instead of guessing. An EMI depends on the principal, the rate, the tenure, the schedule generation rules, the rounding policy, the treatment of rate changes and part-payments, and the dates on which each of those applies. A defect in any one of those, affecting only a narrow combination, produces exactly this symptom: a small subset wrong by a small amount, month after month. The case also tests the recovery discipline: correcting the schedule is not enough, because customers have already paid the wrong amount and the difference must be handled through a controlled adjustment, not a silent fix.
solution:
Start by defining the affected population precisely: list every complaining account and search for others with the same characteristics, so the fix covers silent cases as well as complaints. For each affected loan, capture the full calculation inputs: principal, sanctioned rate, rate change history with effective dates, tenure, schedule generation rules, rounding policy, part-payment history, and the dates each input applied. Then run the same inputs through an independent calculation and compare the result with the system schedule, line by line, so the first point of divergence is visible.

Segment the divergences by cause: a rate change applied from the wrong date, a part-payment that did not re-amortise the schedule, a rounding rule applied at the wrong step, or a date rule that mishandles month ends and short months. Confirm each cause against the product terms and the rate table version in force on the relevant date, and check the unaffected population to confirm the cause explains why they are correct. Fix the cause, regenerate only the affected schedules, and validate the new schedules against the independent calculation before release. Then correct the customer impact through a controlled adjustment: compute the difference paid to date for each account, apply the adjustment with a linked reference and a clear customer statement, and confirm the new EMI and the remaining tenure in writing. Record the root cause, the population, the fix and the adjustment evidence for audit.

decision.question: Aldergate Bank receives complaints from a small group of loan customers whose monthly EMI is wrong. Most customers are unaffected. The affected loans share dates, rate changes or part-payments, and three teams hold three different theories. You are the business analyst asked to find the cause and define the correction.

options.label: A
options.detail: Tell affected customers the difference is immaterial and close the complaints.

options.label: B
options.detail: Apply a rounding fix to all loans, since rounding is the most likely cause of a small EMI error.

options.label: C
options.detail: Regenerate every schedule in the portfolio, since a full rebuild will fix the affected subset too.

options.label: D
options.detail: Trace the calculation for affected and unaffected loans through product terms, rate tables, rounding, dates, schedule generation and customer data, then correct the cause and adjust affected accounts through a controlled process.

decisionRationale: Option D is correct because a subset-only error needs a traced comparison between affected and unaffected cases, not a blanket fix. Option B assumes the cause without evidence and may change correct schedules. Option C rebuilds correct schedules and risks introducing new errors. Option A ignores a real financial error that compounds every month.

steps.title: Log complaints and identify the full affected population
Capture calculation inputs for affected and unaffected loans
Confirm product terms and rate table versions with effective dates
Run an independent calculation and find the first point of divergence
Fix the cause and regenerate only the affected schedules
Compute and apply controlled adjustments with linked references
Notify each affected customer with the corrected EMI and the adjustment

happy: Each affected loan has a corrected schedule that matches an independent calculation, the difference paid to date is adjusted through a controlled process with a linked reference, and every affected customer receives a clear statement of the corrected EMI and the adjustment. The root cause is fixed so no new loans take the wrong path, and the silent cases found by the population search are corrected too.

negative.title: Rate change applied from the wrong date
negative.detail: A rate change takes effect a month late, so the EMI uses the old rate for one instalment. Correct the effective date rule, regenerate the affected schedules, and adjust the difference.

negative.title: Part-payment does not re-amortise
negative.detail: A part-payment reduces the balance but the schedule keeps the old EMI. Apply the product rule for part-payments, regenerate the schedule, and confirm the new EMI with the customer.

negative.title: Rounding applied at the wrong step
negative.detail: Rounding the interest before the EMI is derived shifts the instalment by a small amount each month. Apply rounding at the step the product terms define, and validate against the independent calculation.

negative.title: Month-end date rule mishandled
negative.detail: A loan starting on the 31st produces a wrong first instalment date. Correct the date rule for short months and validate the first instalment date for affected loans.

technical: Store the calculation inputs with their source, version and effective date: product terms version, rate table version, schedule generation rules, rounding policy and the customer data snapshot used. Keep the independent calculation workbook with the comparison that shows the first point of divergence, and log every schedule regeneration and every adjustment with account, operator, timestamp, old and new values and checker. Preserve the original schedule alongside the corrected one so the change is auditable, and keep the adjustment reference linked to the loan account.

accounting: An incorrect EMI is a direct financial error: the customer pays too much or too little each month, and the difference accumulates in the loan balance and the interest charged. The correction must therefore be a controlled financial adjustment, not a silent schedule change: compute the difference to date, post the adjustment with a linked reference, and reconcile the adjusted balances to the corrected schedules. Operations need a worklist of affected accounts with the adjustment amount, the approval status and the customer notification status, and a service level for completing the corrections. The interest effect of the error must be included in the adjustment, and finance must confirm the total value corrected.

scenarios.then: the new rate applies from the correct date and the EMI is validated against an independent calculation.

questions.question: Why is a blanket rounding fix the wrong first step?
options: The cause is unproven and a blanket fix may change correct schedules
questions.explanation: A subset-only error needs a traced comparison; an unproven blanket fix risks breaking the majority of correct schedules.

questions.question: What does an independent calculation provide?
options: A comparison that shows the first point where the system calculation diverges
questions.explanation: Running the same inputs through an independent calculation exposes the first step where the system result differs.

questions.question: Why must silent cases be found, not only complaints?
options: Loans with the same characteristics may be wrong without the customer noticing
questions.explanation: Customers may not notice a small monthly error, so the population search must find every loan with the same cause.

questions.question: How should the money already overpaid or underpaid be handled?
options: By asking the customer to pay it back immediately
Through a controlled adjustment with a linked reference and a clear customer statement
By writing it off without a record
questions.explanation: The difference is a real financial error and must be corrected through a controlled, audited adjustment that the customer can see.
